newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Ministers block increase in EU's merger powers.
newsitem.headline: Ministers block increase in EU's merger powers.

text.p: European Union industry ministers rejected unequivocally on Thursday a proposal to increase the European Commission's power to vet mergers and acquisitions.
The Commission wanted to lower the turnover thresholds set in the EU's merger regulation which determine whether a merger or takeover has a Union dimension.

"The main question was whether the delegations could agree to a reduction in the threshold level. I think that is pretty dead," an EU official told reporters after the ministers held an orientation debate on the proposal.

The Commission proposed in July that it should review all mergers involving companies with an aggregate turnover above three billion European currency units ($3.8 billion) worldwide and 150 million each in the Union. The current thresholds are five billion Ecus and 250 million Ecus respectively.
Seven countries opposed the reduction -- Germany, France, Denmark, Spain, Ireland, Sweden and Britain, a diplomat said.
The outcome is no great surprise as the EU's larger states, with the exception of Italy, have always opposed increasing the Commission's already extensive powers in the competition area.

But it is bad news for the business community which had hoped that smaller deals could also be dealt with under the one-stop-shop procedure which allows for operations to clear all regulatory hurdles in the Union within the record time of one month.

Diplomats were equally wary of the chances of a fall-back proposal to allow for deals involving more than three EU national competition authorities, but falling below the thresholds, to be notified to the Commission instead.
Discussions were to continue, they said, but here too the Commission faced an uphill struggle since the ministers agreed that any decision should be taken by unanimity.
The Commission currently reviews an average of 200 mergers and acquisitions a year under a 1990 regulation which bans creation or strengthening of dominant positions.

It has only blocked five such deals, three of them in the media sector due to fears that the dominant companies, especially in the telecommunications and cable television fields, were trying to close the market before competition can bite.
